sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: COVID-OUT reported a lower hazard of later clinician-diagnosed Long COVID after metformin began during acute infection, but the result remains provisional pending correction reconciliation. Its result belongs to prevention, because treatment began before the long-term illness being counted. A reader who already has long COVID faces a different question, and this study cannot supply that answer. This unresolved source-integrity issue prevents treating the reported finding as a settled prevention conclusion. The clinical meaning depends on who entered the study, how a diagnosis was counted, and what later trials found. This draft preserves those boundaries and does not assign an evidence grade or recommend a regimen.

sections.title: Methods
sections.paragraph: The trial used masked random allocation and a factorial design, allowing metformin and matched placebo groups to contain balanced co-treatments. The long-term analysis included 1126 people, while the original randomized population was larger. Those counts answer different questions: assignment describes the trial population, whereas the long-term group describes the participants contributing to this analysis. Eligibility selected adults with overweight or obesity and a recent infection, without a known earlier infection. Our appraisal priority is therefore both internal comparison and applicability. Neither randomization nor a large initial recruitment total automatically makes the result representative of people with different clinical histories.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: ACTIV-6 tested metformin begun during acute infection and did not meet its stated efficacy threshold for symptoms attributed to COVID-19 or death at six months. The secondary participant-reported clinician-diagnosis estimate favored metformin, but its credible interval included no difference. These findings should be read together without swapping their roles. Our interpretation is that the primary result limits the strength of a broad prevention claim, while the secondary finding remains relevant to future investigation. The trial does not test whether metformin treats symptoms in someone who already has long COVID. Keeping that distinction visible makes the evidence useful even when it does not give a simple yes or no.

sections.title: Results
sections.paragraph: The adjusted difference for symptoms attributed to COVID-19 or death at day 180 was −0.8 percentage points, with a 95% credible interval from −2.2 to 0.6. The posterior probability of benefit was 0.83, below the trial's 0.975 threshold. A negative difference favors metformin, but the interval also contains no difference and a small difference in the other direction. Our interpretation is therefore uncertainty about the size and presence of benefit under this study's model, rather than proof of equal outcomes. The secondary clinician-diagnosis estimate also had an interval including no difference and does not override the primary finding. Its intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, so it needs its own cautious, outcome-specific reading.

sections.title: Summary
sections.paragraph: STOP-PASC did not find a significant benefit from a 15-day nirmatrelvir–ritonavir course for its selected long COVID symptoms. The study is relevant to established illness because participants already had persistent symptoms when treatment began. Both groups improved over time, which makes the randomized comparison more informative than a before-and-after story about the active drug alone. Our interpretation is that this regimen did not demonstrate the expected advantage in the enrolled population. The finding does not settle every antiviral, duration, symptom subtype, or possible mechanism. It does challenge a claim that improvement after taking this treatment, by itself, proves a drug effect.

Secondary and exploratory findings need caution because multiple comparisons can generate apparently interesting differences even without a reproducible treatment advantage.

Adverse events and treatment discontinuations were recorded, but a modest trial cannot provide a complete picture of rare harms or risks in excluded patients. Our review therefore keeps harms visible alongside the absence of demonstrated benefit. It also separates study exclusions from medical contraindications: the latter require current product-specific authoritative information and qualified clinical interpretation. There is no dosing recommendation in this review and no inference that a longer course would work.

sections.paragraph: The pilot did not demonstrate a between-group clinical benefit on UPDRS total, despite improvement within the metformin arm.

sections.title: Design and population
sections.paragraph: Prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled adjunctive pilot trial; per-protocol analysis. Adults aged at least 50 years with Parkinson's disease receiving levodopa/carbidopa; diabetes and several other conditions excluded; single center in Egypt. 60 randomized, 30 per arm. Results analyzed 27 metformin and 25 control after 3 and 5 withdrawals respectively (pp3–6). Metformin 500 mg twice daily is dose, not sample size.

sections.title: Extracted outcomes
sections.paragraph: Primary UPDRS total at 3 months: Metformin median (IQR) 152 (129–166) at baseline and 128 (98–151) after treatment; control 141 (115–164) and 139 (101–151.5). Between-group post-treatment P=0.515, rank-biserial r=0.106. Within-metformin P=0.001 is not evidence of superiority to control. (PDF p6 Table2; p7 Results). Clinical subscores: All between-group post-treatment tests nonsignificant: mentation/behavior/mood P=0.195, activities of daily living P=0.441, motor examination P=0.426, therapy complications P=0.705, Schwab/England P=0.137, modified Hoehn/Yahr P=0.082. (PDF p6 Table2). Biomarkers after 3 months: Between-group differences were reported for alpha-synuclein, BDNF, HMGB-1 and TLR4 (PDF p7 Table3). Units for all biomarker estimates are not fully represented in the accepted extraction, so their numerical magnitudes are withheld here. Biomarker differences do not establish clinical superiority. Reported adverse effects: Metformin/control counts: nausea 6/5, diarrhea 4/2, vomiting 5/3, hypotension 9/5, delusions 5/3, abdominal pain 8/5, with arm denominators 27/25. All reported comparisons P>0.05; this small study does not establish equivalent safety. (PDF p8 Table4).

sections.title: Stated limitations
sections.paragraph: Short duration, small sample, one metformin dose, single center/Middle East population; metabolic rate and dietary habits not measured/controlled; further biomarker and vitamin B12/lipid/glucose assessment desirable (pp8–9).

sections.title: Source summary
sections.paragraph: The report describes exploratory metabolic and brain-connectivity findings, but the accepted record has no current between-arm cognitive efficacy estimate.

sections.title: Design and population
sections.paragraph: Exploratory post hoc metabolomic and imaging analysis of an open-label randomized 24-week trial. Clinically stable schizophrenia, disease duration at most 5 years, receiving antipsychotics alone or metformin add-on at a Chinese center; median age 22 years. Parent trial 72 randomized (control:metformin 1:2). Current plasma/follow-up analysis 58:40 metformin,18 control. MRI initial eligible41; final analysis33:21 metformin,12 control (pp3–4,6). Metformin1500 mg/day is dose, not n.

sections.title: Extracted outcomes
sections.paragraph: Between-group metabolite differences at week24: Baseline-adjusted least-square mean differences (95% CI), μg/mL: oxaloacetic acid0.87(0.61,1.13); citric acid4.40(3.35,5.45); isocitric acid0.50(0.37,0.63); alpha-ketoglutaric acid0.56(0.41,0.71); succinic acid5.77(4.03,7.51); fumaric acid0.45(0.28,0.63); malic acid0.27(0.19,0.35); lactic acid−148.09(−184.61,−111.57); pyruvic acid−38.17(−47.18,−29.17); all P<0.001. (PDF p8 Table3 week24). Hippocampal functional connectivity: Left caudal hippocampus/right medio-ventral occipital cortex difference−0.334 at week12; right caudal hippocampus/right middle frontal gyrus difference0.284 at week24; both P<0.001. (PDF p7 Results; Fig1 p5). Exploratory cognition correlations: Week12 working-memory change correlated with alpha-ketoglutaric acid r=0.34, succinic acid r=0.36, lactic acid r=0.34 (P<0.05); week24 verbal learning negatively correlated with alpha-ketoglutaric acid r=−0.49 and fumaric acid r=−0.48 (P<0.01). These are associations, not proof of mediation. (PDF p7 Results; Fig2 p8). Treatment interaction and null findings: Only the week12 succinic-acid change×treatment interaction for week24 working memory reached P=0.0193; other tested interactive effects were not statistically significant. Negative relationship for the significant interaction discussed. Current numerical cognitive between-arm efficacy estimate NOT IN CORPUS; prior report cited. (PDF pp8,10; p7 opening cognition paragraph).

sections.title: Stated limitations
sections.paragraph: Small sample, incomplete blood/MRI time points, potential confounding and medication-adherence bias, short follow-up, mechanism incompletely explored (pp10–11). Methods explicitly use unadjusted exploratory correlation/interaction P values and last observation carried forward for missing TCA/cognition; MRI not imputed (p4).
